questions.stem: The word "biology" is derived from two Greek words "bios" and "logos". The meaning of the word "logos" is
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.1): biology comes from the Greek 'bios' (life) and 'logos' (study or knowledge), so biology is the study of life.
'Logos' = study of. Answer: C. (A is the meaning of 'bios'.)
tips: The ending '-logy' in any science (ecology, cytology, zoology) means 'study of'.

similar_questions.stem: The branch of biology that studies cells is
explanation_steps: 'Cyto-' = cell and '-logy' = study of, so cytology is the study of cells. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Prokaryotic types of cells are found in
explanation_steps: Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus; they are found in bacteria (kingdom Monera, including cyanobacteria) (G9 p.17).
Animals and plants are eukaryotes, and viruses are not cells at all (no cytoplasm, no cell membrane), so E is wrong. Answer: D.
tips: Viruses are acellular: they are neither prokaryotic nor eukaryotic.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following organisms has eukaryotic cells?
explanation_steps: Amoeba is a protist with a true nucleus (eukaryote). E. coli, cyanobacteria and Streptococcus are bacteria (prokaryotes); a virus is not a cell. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Organisms are grouped in the following ranks. Which rank groups the organisms with their least similarity?
explanation_steps: The taxonomic ranks are kingdom → phylum → class → order → family → genus → species (G9 p.54).

The higher the rank, the more organisms it contains and the fewer features they share. Kingdom is the highest rank given, so its members are least similar. Answer: B. (Species members are most similar.)
tips: Memory aid: 'King Philip Came Over For Good Soup' – similarity increases towards Species.

similar_questions.stem: Which pair of organisms is most closely related?

options.A: Two members of the same kingdom
options.B: Two members of the same class
options.C: Two members of the same order
options.D: Two members of the same genus
options.E: Two members of the same phylum

explanation_steps: Genus is the lowest rank listed, so its members share the most features. Answer: D.

questions.stem: The following are types of asexual reproduction in animals, except
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.88): 'Some animals are also capable of asexual reproduction, which may take place through regeneration, parthenogenesis or budding.'
Binary fission (one cell splitting into two) is the typical asexual reproduction of bacteria and protists, and it is not listed for animals. Answer: B.
E ('None of the above') is also accepted, because a few animals (some flatworms and sea anemones) do reproduce by fission, and the examiner may have counted all four as animal methods.
tips: Parthenogenesis is the common trap: it involves an egg, but the egg is not fertilised, so it counts as asexual in the textbook.

similar_questions.stem: The development of a new organism from an unfertilised egg is called
explanation_steps: Parthenogenesis: an unfertilised mature egg is activated and develops into a new individual (e.g. drone honeybees). Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: The textbook lists regeneration, parthenogenesis and budding for animals, so B (binary fission, a bacterial/protist method) is keyed; E also accepted because some animals reproduce by fission. Teacher to confirm.

questions.stem: Hydrophyte plants that live totally under water are called
explanation_steps: Hydrophytes (water plants) are grouped as floating, submerged (submergent) and emergent plants (G9 p.144).

Submergent plants live completely under the water surface; emergent plants are rooted in water with shoots above it; floating plants float on the surface. Succulents are xerophytes and halophytes live in salty soil. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: A plant rooted in shallow water whose leaves and flowers rise above the water surface is
explanation_steps: Rooted underwater with shoots in the air = emergent plant (e.g. reeds, papyrus). Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a behavioral adaptation of animals?
explanation_steps: Adaptations may be structural (body parts: thick fur, long neck, large ears), physiological (body functions, e.g. sharp vision) or behavioural (what the animal does) (G9 pp.149–150).
Pretending to be dead (playing dead to avoid a predator) is an action, so it is behavioural. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a behavioural adaptation?
explanation_steps: Migration is something the animal does; the others are body structures. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The process by which polysaccharides are formed is
explanation_steps: Monosaccharides join by glycosidic bonds with the removal of a water molecule for each bond; this is a condensation (dehydration-synthesis) reaction (G10 p.3).
Condensation and dehydration synthesis are two names for the same process, so the best answer is E (A and D). Hydrolysis is the reverse (breaking down with water).
tips: Condensation = dehydration synthesis (builds polymers, releases water); hydrolysis = splitting by adding water.

similar_questions.stem: When a disaccharide such as maltose is digested into two glucose molecules, the reaction is
explanation_steps: Breaking a glycosidic bond requires adding water: hydrolysis. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Algae and fungi live together in lichens. The contribution of the fungi in this mutualistic relationship is to
explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p.106): 'The algae produce food by photosynthesis and the fungi obtain water and minerals, and provide attachment for the lichen.'
So the fungus contributes B and C. Answer: E. (A is the alga's contribution.)

similar_questions.stem: The relationship between nitrogen-fixing bacteria and the root nodules of legumes is an example of
explanation_steps: Both benefit: the bacteria get food and shelter, the plant gets fixed nitrogen. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not made up of protein?
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.8): 'Proteins are structural components of plasma membrane, hair, nails and skeletal muscles. Enzymes and some hormones are proteins.'

Hair and nails (keratin) and enzymes are proteins, but only some hormones are (insulin, growth hormone); steroid hormones such as oestrogen, testosterone and aldosterone are lipids and thyroxine is an amino-acid derivative. So 'hormone' is the item that is not (necessarily) made of protein. Answer: D.
E is also accepted, because the examiner may have counted hormones as proteins.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following hormones is a steroid (lipid), not a protein?
explanation_steps: Testosterone is a steroid made from cholesterol; the others are proteins or peptides. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Hair, nails and enzymes are proteins; the textbook says only 'some hormones are proteins', so D is keyed. E ('None of the above') accepted in case the examiner counted hormones as proteins. Teacher to confirm.

questions.stem: Vitamin K is most important for
explanation_steps: Vitamin K is needed by the liver to make prothrombin and other clotting factors; lack of it causes slow blood clotting and bleeding (G10 pp.14, 74–76).
Answer: D.
tips: 'K' for 'Koagulation' (German) – the clotting vitamin.

similar_questions.stem: Night blindness is caused by a deficiency of
explanation_steps: Vitamin A is needed to make the visual pigment of the rods; lack of it causes night blindness. Answer: A.

questions.stem: The Lymphatic System consists of all of the following, except
explanation_steps: Lymph is tissue fluid (mostly water with dissolved substances) that drains into lymph vessels; it contains white blood cells (leukocytes), especially lymphocytes, and lymph nodes contain macrophages (G10 pp.85–87).
Red blood cells are too large to leave the capillaries, so they are not part of lymph or the lymphatic system. Answer: D.
tips: Lymph = plasma-like fluid without red cells (and with fewer proteins).

similar_questions.stem: Which organ belongs to the lymphatic system?
explanation_steps: The spleen, tonsils, thymus and lymph nodes are lymphatic organs. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The tube-like structure that allows entry of additional air through the mouth is
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.109): the pharynx is part of both the respiratory and digestive systems; 'this allows the entry of additional air through the mouth when it is required and also allows the passage of air when the nose is blocked.'
Answer: B.
tips: The pharynx (throat) is the crossroads of the air and food passages.

similar_questions.stem: The flap of tissue that closes the glottis during swallowing is the
explanation_steps: The epiglottis covers the glottis so that food goes into the oesophagus, not the trachea. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following represents the peripheral nervous system?
explanation_steps: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord (A, B, C and E are all parts of the brain/CNS). The peripheral nervous system is made of the nerves outside the CNS: 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves (G10 pp.170, 176–177).
Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: How many pairs of spinal nerves are there in humans?
explanation_steps: Humans have 31 pairs of spinal nerves and 12 pairs of cranial nerves. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Some people can have a problem in reading books because they cannot contract their
explanation_steps: To focus on near objects (accommodation) the ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments slacken and the lens becomes thicker (G10 p.150).
If the ciliary muscles cannot contract (e.g. in old age – presbyopia), near vision such as reading becomes blurred. Answer: B.
The iris and pupil control the amount of light entering the eye, not focusing.

similar_questions.stem: When the eye looks at a distant object, the ciliary muscles

options.A: contract and the lens becomes thicker
options.B: relax and the lens becomes thinner
options.C: contract and the lens becomes thinner
options.D: relax and the lens becomes thicker

explanation_steps: For distant vision the ciliary muscles relax, the ligaments pull tight and the lens is thin (long focal length). Answer: B.

questions.stem: The epididymis, vas deferens and urethra, are a series of ducts found in ______ body system.
explanation_steps: Sperm pass from the testis to the epididymis (storage), then the vas deferens (sperm duct) and finally the urethra – the male reproductive ducts (G11 pp.28–29).
(The urethra is shared with the excretory system, but the epididymis and vas deferens are purely reproductive.) Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Where are sperm cells produced?
explanation_steps: Sperm are made in the seminiferous tubules and stored/matured in the epididymis. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following female reproductive structures is responsible for egg production?
explanation_steps: The ovaries are the female gonads: they produce eggs (ova) and the hormones oestrogen and progesterone (G11 p.27).
The Fallopian tube carries the egg (and is the site of fertilisation); the uterus holds the developing fetus. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Fertilisation normally takes place in the
explanation_steps: The egg meets the sperm in the upper part of the oviduct. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Pores on a leaf surface that function in gas exchange are called
explanation_steps: Stomata are pores in the leaf epidermis, each surrounded by two guard cells; CO₂ enters and O₂ and water vapour leave through them (G11 p.127).
Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: The cells that open and close a stoma are
explanation_steps: Guard cells change shape as they gain or lose water, opening or closing the pore. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Color blindness is an X-linked recessive trait in humans. In a cross that involves this trait, parents cannot produce a
explanation_steps: Males are XY and have only one X chromosome, so a male is either normal (XᴮY) or colour blind (XᵇY); he cannot be a heterozygous carrier (G12 pp.46–47).
Carrier daughters (XᴮXᵇ), colour-blind sons, colour-blind daughters (XᵇXᵇ, from a carrier mother and colour-blind father) and normal sons are all possible. Answer: E.
tips: Carriers of X-linked recessive traits are always female.

similar_questions.stem: A carrier woman (XᴮXᵇ) marries a normal man (XᴮY). What fraction of their sons is expected to be colour blind?
explanation_steps: Sons get their X from the mother: half get Xᴮ (normal), half get Xᵇ (colour blind). So 1/2 of the sons.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not used for birth control?
explanation_steps: The textbook's table of birth-control methods (G11 pp.44–46) includes abstinence, the rhythm method, spermicidal creams and foaming tablets ('the tablet forms a foam that kills sperm cells'), and barriers such as the condom.
All four are used for birth control, so the answer is E (None of the above).

similar_questions.stem: Which birth-control method also gives protection against sexually transmitted infections?
explanation_steps: A condom is a physical barrier that stops body fluids passing between partners. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The process of removing metabolic waste products from the body is called
explanation_steps: Excretion is the removal of metabolic wastes (urea, CO₂, excess salts and water) produced by the body's cells (G10 p.138).
Defecation removes undigested food, which was never part of metabolism, so it is egestion, not excretion; urination is only one form of excretion. Answer: D.
tips: Faeces = egestion (undigested food); urine, sweat and CO₂ = excretion (metabolic wastes).

similar_questions.stem: Which organ excretes carbon dioxide?
explanation_steps: CO₂, a waste of cellular respiration, is breathed out through the lungs. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which statement is correct about viruses?

options.A: Viruses have cytoplasm but not nucleus.
options.B: Viruses have nucleic acids and are capable of metabolism.
options.C: Viruses need to invade a living host cell for multiplication.
options.E: Viruses have nucleus but no cytoplasm.

explanation_steps: A virus is only nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) in a protein coat; it has no cytoplasm, nucleus, cell membrane or metabolism of its own (G9 p.41).
It can reproduce only inside a living host cell, using the host's machinery. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following diseases is caused by a virus?
explanation_steps: Measles is viral; TB, cholera and typhoid are bacterial; malaria is caused by a protozoan (Plasmodium). Answer: C.

questions.stem: The enzyme lipase breaks a lipid molecule into

options.A: two fatty acids and two glycerol molecules.
options.B: one fatty acid and three glycerol molecules.
options.C: one fatty acid and two glycerol molecules.
options.D: three fatty acids and one glycerol molecules.
options.E: two fatty acids and three glycerol molecules.

explanation_steps: A fat (triglyceride) is made of one glycerol molecule joined to three fatty acids (G9 p.121; G10 p.10).
Lipase hydrolyses it into fatty acids and glycerol (G10 pp.37–38): three fatty acids + one glycerol. Answer: D.
tips: 'Tri-glyceride' = three fatty acids on one glycerol.

similar_questions.stem: The end products of protein digestion are
explanation_steps: Proteases (pepsin, trypsin, peptidase) break proteins down into amino acids. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The proteins in the food we eat are mainly used
explanation_steps: Dietary proteins are digested to amino acids, which are used to build new cells and tissues (growth), repair damaged tissues and replace worn-out cells, and to make enzymes, some hormones and antibodies (G10 p.8).
All four uses are correct. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: A child with a swollen belly, oedema and thin limbs, whose diet lacks protein, is suffering from
explanation_steps: Kwashiorkor is protein deficiency; marasmus is overall energy deficiency. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The pressure responsible for making blood flow through the blood vessels is produced by the
explanation_steps: Blood pressure is the force exerted by blood on the vessel walls; it is created by the contraction of the ventricles of the heart (G10 p.54).
Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: A normal resting blood pressure of a young adult is about
explanation_steps: Systolic (ventricles contracting) about 120 mmHg over diastolic (relaxing) about 80 mmHg. Answer: B.

questions.stem: In human adults, under resting conditions, the heart rate is approximately ______ beats per minute.
explanation_steps: The average resting heart rate of an adult is about 70–72 beats per minute (G10 p.54).
Answer: D.
tips: The pulse you feel at the wrist equals the heart rate.

similar_questions.stem: A heart beats 72 times per minute. How long does one cardiac cycle last?
explanation_steps: Time per beat = 60 s / 72 = 0.83 s.

questions.stem: The types of blood cells that help repair damaged blood vessels are
explanation_steps: Platelets (thrombocytes) stick to the damaged vessel wall, form a plug and release factors that start blood clotting, which seals the damage (G10 pp.71–74).
Granulocytes, neutrophils, basophils and lymphocytes are white blood cells used in defence. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: The protein threads that trap blood cells to form a clot are made of
explanation_steps: Thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads, which form the mesh of the clot. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Gaseous exchange in humans occurs in the
explanation_steps: In humans, O₂ and CO₂ are exchanged across the thin, moist walls of the alveoli of the lungs, which are surrounded by capillaries (G10 p.115).
Human skin exchanges only negligible amounts of gas (unlike frogs). Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Which feature does NOT help alveoli in gas exchange?
explanation_steps: Cartilage rings support the trachea and bronchi; they are not part of alveoli and do not aid diffusion. Answer: E.

questions.stem: The function of the growth hormone (GH) is to

options.A: promote normal skeletal and muscular growth.
options.C: regulate the rate at which amino acids enter the cells.
options.D: stimulate the thyroid gland to produce hormones.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.3): 'The growth hormone (GH) ... promotes normal skeletal and muscular growth by regulating cell division, protein synthesis, and bone growth. It stimulates the rate at which amino acids enter cells, stimulating protein synthesis.'
So both A and C are functions of GH. B is done by FSH/LH and D by TSH. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Over-secretion of growth hormone during childhood causes
explanation_steps: Too much GH in childhood → gigantism; in adulthood → acromegaly; too little in childhood → dwarfism. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Most of the blood components are made in the
explanation_steps: Red blood cells, most white blood cells and platelets are produced in the red bone marrow inside bones (G10 pp.67–70; G11 p.55).
Answer: B.
tips: Making blood cells in bone marrow is one of the functions of the skeleton.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of the skeleton?
explanation_steps: The skeleton supports, protects, makes blood cells and stores calcium and phosphate; it does not make digestive enzymes. Answer: E.

questions.stem: Phalanges are bones found in the human
explanation_steps: Phalanges are the bones of the fingers and toes: 14 in each hand and 14 in each foot (G11 pp.65–66).
So they are found in both the hand and the foot. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: The bones of the palm of the hand are the
explanation_steps: Wrist = carpals, palm = metacarpals, fingers = phalanges (ankle = tarsals, sole = metatarsals). Answer: B.

questions.stem: Joints that are found in the knees, elbows and fingers are examples of a
explanation_steps: Hinge joints allow movement in one plane only, like a door hinge: the knee, the elbow and the joints between the phalanges (G11 pp.68–69).
Ball and socket: shoulder and hip; pivot: between atlas and axis; gliding: between carpals. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: The shoulder and hip joints are examples of
explanation_steps: They allow movement in all directions: ball and socket joints. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Option B is misprinted 'hing joint' (hinge joint); the meaning is clear.

questions.stem: Vasodilation is a mechanism of
explanation_steps: When the body is too hot, arterioles in the skin dilate (vasodilation), so more blood flows near the skin surface and loses heat by radiation (G11 pp.95–96).
Vasoconstriction does the opposite (heat conservation). Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following helps the body to gain or conserve heat?
explanation_steps: Shivering (rapid muscle contractions) produces heat. Sweating, vasodilation and panting lose heat. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) has an effect on the
explanation_steps: ADH (vasopressin), released by the posterior pituitary, makes the distal tubules and collecting ducts of the kidney nephrons more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed and less urine is made (G11 pp.4, 84).
Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: On a very hot day with heavy sweating, the ADH level in the blood
explanation_steps: Water loss raises blood concentration, so more ADH is released and more water is reabsorbed: small volume of concentrated urine. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Homologous structures in vertebrate forelimbs are examples of evidence for evolution from
explanation_steps: Homologous structures (the forelimbs of humans, whales, bats and birds) have the same basic bone pattern but different functions; they show common ancestry and belong to the evidence from comparative anatomy (G12 pp.70–71).
Answer: D.
tips: Homologous = same structure, different function (divergent evolution); analogous = same function, different structure (bird wing and insect wing).

similar_questions.stem: The wing of a bird and the wing of an insect are
explanation_steps: They do the same job (flight) but have completely different structure and origin: analogous. Answer: B.

questions.stem: A source of genetic variation that results due to chromosomal mutation is referred to as
explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p.78): 'Polyploidy is a type of chromosomal mutation. It is the duplication of chromosome sets that results in individuals having more than two of each chromosome.'
Gene mutation is a change within one gene; gene flow is migration of alleles; recombination is reshuffling during meiosis. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: An organism with four complete sets of chromosomes (4n) is described as
explanation_steps: 4n = four sets = tetraploid, a type of polyploidy. Answer: D.

questions.stem: Chemistry is the study of the
explanation_steps: Chemistry is the branch of science that studies the composition, structure and properties of matter and the changes (transformations) that matter undergoes (G9 p.1).
A, B, C and D are all parts of the definition. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a chemical change?
explanation_steps: Rusting forms a new substance (hydrated iron(III) oxide); the others change only state or shape. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following atoms has 7 neutrons?
explanation_steps: Number of neutrons = mass number A − atomic number Z (G9 p.44).
⁵₂He: 5 − 2 = 3; ¹³₆C: 13 − 6 = 7; ⁷₃Li: 7 − 3 = 4; ¹⁵₇N: 15 − 7 = 8; ¹⁶₈O: 16 − 8 = 8. Answer: B. (¹⁵₇N is the trap: 7 is its number of protons.)
tips: The top number is protons + neutrons; the bottom number is protons.

similar_questions.stem: How many neutrons are in an atom of ³⁷₁₇Cl?
explanation_steps: N = A − Z = 37 − 17 = 20 neutrons.

questions.stem: The empirical formula of N₂H₄ is
explanation_steps: The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms (G9 pp.104–106).
N₂H₄ (hydrazine): N : H = 2 : 4 = 1 : 2 → NH₂. Answer: C. (N₂H₄ is the molecular formula.)

similar_questions.stem: The empirical formula of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, is
explanation_steps: Divide by the highest common factor 6: CH₂O. Answer: B.

questions.stem: In the Periodic Table, the elements in group IA are called
explanation_steps: Group IA (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr) = alkali metals; group IIA = alkaline earth metals (G10 p.15).
Alkanes, alkenes and alkynes are hydrocarbons, not groups of the periodic table. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Group VIIA elements (F, Cl, Br, I) are called
explanation_steps: Group VIIA = halogens ('salt formers'). Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following forces is categorized as intramolecular force?
explanation_steps: Intramolecular forces are the chemical bonds that hold atoms together: ionic, covalent and metallic bonds. Intermolecular forces act between molecules: hydrogen bonds, dipole–dipole, ion–dipole and dispersion (van der Waals) forces (G10 pp.41–42, 58–61).
Answer: D.
tips: 'Intra' = within (bonds); 'inter' = between (much weaker attractions).

similar_questions.stem: Which force explains why ice floats and water has a high boiling point?
explanation_steps: Hydrogen bonds between H₂O molecules raise the boiling point and give ice an open, less dense structure. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following mixtures represents a liquid-solid solution?
explanation_steps: Solutions are classified by the states of solute and solvent (G10 p.64, Table 3.1). A liquid solute in a solid solvent: liquid mercury in solid silver = silver amalgam (dental filling).
Sand + water is a heterogeneous mixture (not a solution); N₂ + O₂ is gas–gas (air); Fe + C is solid–solid (steel); water + ethanol is liquid–liquid. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Carbonated soft drink (CO₂ dissolved in water) is an example of a
explanation_steps: The solute CO₂ is a gas and the solvent water is a liquid. Answer: A.

questions.stem: Some fruits like lemon, raw grapes, oranges, etc., have a sour taste due to the presence of
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.123): 'Citrus fruits such as lemons and oranges contain citric acid.'
Acetic acid – vinegar; lactic acid – sour milk; hydrochloric acid – gastric juice. Answer: B. (Raw grapes contain mainly tartaric and malic acids, but citric acid is the intended answer.)

similar_questions.stem: The acid present in vinegar is
explanation_steps: Vinegar is a dilute solution of acetic acid, CH₃COOH. Answer: B.

questions.stem: One calorie equals to
explanation_steps: A calorie is the heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 g of water by 1 °C; 1 cal = 4.184 J (G10 p.155).
Rounded, 1 cal ≈ 4.2 J. Answer: D. (4200 J = 1 kcal, not 4200 kJ; 8.14 J is a distractor that looks like 8.314, the gas constant.)

questions.stem: Which of the following factors affects the rate of a reaction?

options.D: Concentration of the reactants in a solution

explanation_steps: The factors that affect reaction rate are the nature of the reactants, concentration (or pressure for gases), temperature, surface area (particle size) and catalysts (G11 p.8).
All four listed factors apply. Answer: E.
tips: Most rate factors work by increasing the number of effective collisions per second.

similar_questions.stem: Powdered marble reacts faster with hydrochloric acid than marble chips because
explanation_steps: Powder exposes more surface to the acid, so more collisions occur per second. Answer: B.

questions.stem: It is very risky to stay in a closed room while charcoal is burning because it produces the poisonous gas ______ that causes death.
explanation_steps: When charcoal (carbon) burns in a limited supply of air (a closed room), incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide: 2C + O₂ → 2CO (G11 p.77).
CO combines with haemoglobin much more strongly than oxygen, so blood can no longer carry O₂ – it is colourless, odourless and deadly. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which metal can displace copper from copper(II) sulphate solution?

explanation_steps: Gas particles are far apart and move freely and fast, so gases have no definite shape or volume, diffuse quickly, are easily compressed and expand strongly on heating (G9 p.7).
Because the particles are far apart, gases have a LOW density. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Which state of matter has a definite volume but no definite shape?

explanation_steps: Valence electrons: B has 3, each F has 7; total = 3 + 3 × 7 = 24 electrons = 12 pairs (G12 pp.1–4).
B forms three single B–F bonds (3 bonding pairs, B has no lone pair). The remaining 9 pairs are lone pairs, three on each F. Answer: D.

explanation_steps: Z = 17 → electron configuration 2, 8, 7 (chlorine). It needs one electron to complete its octet, so it forms X⁻ (G10 p.42).
The ion has 17 + 1 = 18 electrons. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: How many electrons does a magnesium ion Mg²⁺ have? [Z(Mg) = 12]

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct about elements and their chemical symbols?

options.A: Each element has a unique name and a chemical symbol.
options.B: All letters of chemical symbols are capitalized.
options.C: Most chemical symbols of elements are derived from Latin names.
options.D: Chemical symbols of elements have a maximum of two letters.
options.E: Chemical symbols of all elements begin with different letters.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.80): 'Each element has a unique chemical name and symbol. The chemical symbol consists of one, two, or three letters.' Only the first letter is capital.
The symbols for most elements come from their English names; only a few (Na, K, Fe, Cu, Ag, Au, Pb…) come from Latin. Many symbols share a first letter (C, Ca, Cl, Co, Cu). Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: The symbol of potassium, K, comes from its Latin name
explanation_steps: Kalium → K; natrium → Na, ferrum → Fe, cuprum → Cu, plumbum → Pb. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following elements is a transition element? [Atomic number: H = 1, Mg = 12, Cl = 17, Ar = 18, Cu = 29]
explanation_steps: Transition elements are the d-block elements (Z = 21–30 in period 4), whose d orbitals are being filled (G10 pp.14, 22–23).
Cu (Z = 29): [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ – a d-block element. H is group IA, Mg IIA, Cl VIIA and Ar VIIIA (all main-group). Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a transition element? [Z: Fe = 26, Zn = 30, Ca = 20, Cr = 24, Mn = 25]
explanation_steps: Ca (Z = 20) is an s-block alkaline earth metal; Cr, Mn, Fe and Zn are in the d block (Z 21–30). Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a quantitative expression of a solution?
explanation_steps: Concentration is the general property being described; its quantitative expressions are mass percent, volume percent, molarity, molality and normality (G10 p.75).
'Concentration' alone is the thing measured, not a quantitative expression of it (and it can be stated qualitatively as 'dilute' or 'concentrated'). Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution containing 0.50 mol of NaCl in 250 mL of solution?

questions.review_flag: Wording: all options are ways of describing concentration; E ('Concentration') is keyed as the general term rather than a quantitative expression. Teacher to confirm.

questions.stem: Until the early 19th century, the sources of organic compounds were believed to be
explanation_steps: Before Wöhler synthesised urea from ammonium cyanate in 1828, the 'vital force' theory held that organic compounds could only be made by living organisms (G12 p.25).
Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Who first made an organic compound (urea) from an inorganic compound, disproving the vital force theory?
explanation_steps: Friedrich Wöhler (1828) heated ammonium cyanate and obtained urea. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Farmers neutralize the effect of acidity of a soil by adding
explanation_steps: Lime (calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide, or limestone CaCO₃) is a base; it neutralises acidic soil (G10 p.132).
Acetic acid would make the soil more acidic; calamine lotion treats insect stings; NaCl is neutral. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: A bee sting is acidic. Which substance is best rubbed on it?
explanation_steps: A weak base such as baking soda (NaHCO₃) neutralises the acid. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Cooking food is an example of
explanation_steps: An endothermic reaction absorbs heat from the surroundings (ΔH > 0) (G10 p.158).
Cooking needs a continuous supply of heat for the chemical changes in the food to take place, so it is endothermic (and irreversible). Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is an exothermic process?
explanation_steps: Combustion releases heat (ΔH < 0). The others absorb heat. Answer: C.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of Cl in KClO₄?
explanation_steps: K = +1, O = −2 and the compound is neutral (G11 pp.30–32).

questions.stem: In general, nonmetals

options.A: are naturally solids at room temperature.
options.B: are non-lustrous and cannot be polished.
options.D: are good conductors of heat and electricity, except graphite.

explanation_steps: General properties of non-metals (G9 p.23): dull (non-lustrous, cannot be polished), brittle when solid, poor conductors of heat and electricity (graphite is the exception), low densities; many are gases (O₂, N₂) and bromine is a liquid.
A, C, D and E describe metals or single exceptions. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Which non-metal is a liquid at room temperature?
explanation_steps: Bromine is the only non-metal that is liquid at room temperature (mercury is the liquid metal). Answer: C.

explanation_steps: Very unreactive metals such as gold and platinum occur free (uncombined, native) in nature; reactive metals (K, Mg, Zn) occur only as compounds in ores (G11 pp.121–125).
Copper is found mostly combined (sulphide ores), though small amounts of native copper exist, so platinum is the best answer. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Why is sodium never found free in nature?
explanation_steps: Sodium reacts readily with oxygen and water, so it exists only in compounds (e.g. NaCl). Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not correct about a solution?

options.A: Sedimentation of the particles does not occur in a solution.
options.B: A solution is clear and transparent.
options.C: The composition of a solution is fixed.
options.D: Components of a solution could not be separated by filtration.
options.E: Size of the dissolved solute is in its molecular or ionic form.

explanation_steps: A solution is a homogeneous mixture: its particles are molecules or ions, it is clear, it does not settle and cannot be separated by filtration (G10 pp.64–65).
Like every mixture, its composition is variable (you can dissolve more or less solute), not fixed. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Which mixture shows the Tyndall effect (scatters a beam of light)?
explanation_steps: Colloids such as milk scatter light; true solutions do not. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct order of the atomic radii of the elements? [Atomic number: N = 7, O = 8, F = 9]
explanation_steps: N, O and F are in period 2. Across a period the nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell, so atomic radius decreases (G10 pp.24–25).
Radius: N > O > F, i.e. F < O < N. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which atom is the largest? [Z: Li = 3, Na = 11, K = 19, Be = 4, Mg = 12]
explanation_steps: Radius increases down a group (more shells) and decreases across a period; K is lowest in group IA. Answer: C.

questions.stem: One of the threats to the Earth's surface is "global warming", which is mainly caused due to an increase in the amount of
explanation_steps: Carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels and deforestation is the main greenhouse gas: it traps infrared radiation from the Earth and raises the average temperature (G11 p.83).
SO₂, SO₃ and NO₂ are mainly responsible for acid rain. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Acid rain is mainly caused by
explanation_steps: Sulphur and nitrogen oxides dissolve in rain water forming H₂SO₄ and HNO₃. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an alkane that has four carbon atoms?
explanation_steps: Alkane names show the number of carbons: meth- 1, eth- 2, prop- 3, but- 4, pent- 5, hex- 6 (G12 p.37).
Butane, C₄H₁₀. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: What is the molecular formula of pentane?
explanation_steps: Alkanes are CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; n = 5 → C₅H₁₂.

questions.stem: Which of the following physical quantities is a vector quantity?
questions.image_alt: Table 'Constants that you may require for questions 71-100': acceleration due to gravity g = 10 m/s²; velocity of light in air and free space c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s; elementary charge e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; Coulomb constant k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²; Planck's constant h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s; permeability of free space μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m·A⁻¹; density of water ρw = 1000 kg/m³.
explanation_steps: A vector has magnitude and direction; a scalar has magnitude only (G9 pp.47–48).
Displacement (change of position in a given direction) is a vector. Mass, speed, energy and distance are scalars. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a scalar quantity?
explanation_steps: Work (energy) has no direction; force, velocity, acceleration and momentum are vectors. Answer: D.

questions.stem: The correct symbol representation for the SI unit of mass is
explanation_steps: The SI unit of mass is the kilogram, symbol kg: prefix k (kilo) in lower case and g for gram (G9 pp.7–8).
Unit symbols are never pluralised (no 's') and the prefix 'k' is always small (capital K is kelvin). Answer: C.
tips: Symbols named after people are capitalised (N, J, W, K); others are lower case (m, kg, s).

similar_questions.stem: Which is the correct way to write five metres per second?
explanation_steps: The metre is 'm' and the second is 's'; 'ms' would mean millisecond. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The positions of five objects A, B, C, D and E along the x-axis are: xA = 4 m, xB = -4 m, xC = 7 m, xD = 2 m and xE = -7 m, respectively. The object that is located nearest to the origin is
explanation_steps: The distance from the origin is the magnitude of the position, |x|; the sign only gives the side (G9 pp.68–69).
|xA| = 4 m, |xB| = 4 m, |xC| = 7 m, |xD| = 2 m, |xE| = 7 m. The smallest is 2 m. Answer: D.
tips: A negative position is not 'smaller' in distance: −7 m is as far away as +7 m.

similar_questions.stem: An object moves from x = −3 m to x = +5 m. What is its displacement?
explanation_steps: Δx = x₂ − x₁ = 5 − (−3) = +8 m (8 m in the +x direction).

questions.stem: The area under the velocity-time graph of an object is numerically equal to the

options.C: change of velocity of the object.

explanation_steps: Area under a v–t graph = velocity × time = displacement (for motion in one direction, the distance travelled) (G9 pp.103–108).
The slope of the v–t graph is the acceleration; the area under an a–t graph is the change in velocity. Answer: E.
tips: Slope of v–t → acceleration; area under v–t → displacement/distance.

similar_questions.stem: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 10 s. How far does it travel?
explanation_steps: Area of the triangle under the v–t graph = ½ × 10 s × 20 m/s = 100 m.

questions.stem: Two forces 8 N and 15 N act concurrently at right angle to each other at the same time. The magnitude of the resultant force, in newtons, is
explanation_steps: For two perpendicular vectors the resultant is found by Pythagoras: R = √(F₁² + F₂²) (G9 pp.54–57).
R = √(8² + 15²) = √(64 + 225) = √289 = 17 N. Answer: A. (23 N would be the sum if they acted in the same direction; 7 N if opposite.)

similar_questions.stem: Two forces of 6 N and 8 N act at right angles on a body. What is the resultant?

questions.stem: According to Newton's First Law, the tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of rest or motion is
explanation_steps: Newton's first law (law of inertia): a body stays at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless a net external force acts on it. The property of resisting a change of motion is inertia (G9 pp.136–138).
Mass is the measure of inertia. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Passengers in a bus fall forward when the bus stops suddenly. This is due to
explanation_steps: Their bodies tend to keep moving forward (inertia of motion) when the bus stops. Answer: B.

questions.stem: A stone of mass 0.200 kg is moving with a speed of 5 m/s. The kinetic energy of the stone, in joules, is
explanation_steps: KE = ½mv² (G9 pp.214–219).
KE = ½ × 0.200 × 5² = 0.1 × 25 = 2.5 J. Answer: C. (5.0 J forgets the ½.)

similar_questions.stem: A 2 kg ball has 64 J of kinetic energy. What is its speed?

questions.stem: If you check an electric bill of the Eritrean Light Power Authority, you will find that the bill is paid for a number of kilowatt-hours (kWh). This shows that the consumed kWh is
explanation_steps: Electrical energy = power × time. A kilowatt-hour is the energy used by a 1 kW appliance in 1 hour: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J (G10 pp.196–199).
So the kWh is a unit of energy, not power. Answer: B.
tips: kW = power; kWh = power × time = energy.

similar_questions.stem: How many joules are in 2 kWh?

questions.stem: A uniform meter rule is pivoted at its center as shown in figure 1. It carries masses of 2 kg and 4 kg at its two ends, respectively. The distance X, in cm, of the 10 kg mass from the pivot in order the meter rule to be balanced is [Figure 1: 2 kg at the left end, 10 kg at distance X to the left of the pivot, 4 kg at the right end; pivot at the 50 cm mark]
questions.image_alt: Figure 1: a uniform meter rule balanced on a pivot (triangle) at its centre. A 2 kg mass hangs from the left end and a 4 kg mass from the right end. A 10 kg mass hangs between the left end and the pivot, at a distance X (marked with a double arrow) to the left of the pivot.
explanation_steps: The rule is uniform and pivoted at its centre, so its own weight has no moment. Each end is 50 cm from the pivot (G10 pp.30–33).
Principle of moments (g cancels): anticlockwise = clockwise → 2 × 50 + 10 × X = 4 × 50.
tips: When g appears on both sides, you can take moments with masses directly.

similar_questions.stem: A uniform metre rule is pivoted at its centre. A 3 kg mass hangs 40 cm to the left of the pivot. Where must a 6 kg mass be hung to balance it?
similar_questions.answer: 20 cm to the right of the pivot
explanation_steps: 3 × 40 = 6 × d → d = 20 cm, on the right-hand side.

questions.stem: In a uniform circular motion like the orbits of the planets and the orbits of natural and communication satellites, the directions of acceleration and force are

options.A: towards the center of the circle.
options.B: away from the center of the circle.
options.C: tangent to the motion of the object.
options.D: parallel to the velocity of the object.
options.E: anti-parallel to the velocity of the object.

explanation_steps: In uniform circular motion the speed is constant but the direction changes, so there is a centripetal acceleration a = v²/r directed towards the centre; by F = ma the net (centripetal) force also points to the centre (G9 pp.148–150).
The velocity is tangential, perpendicular to the acceleration. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: A 2 kg stone is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius 0.5 m at 3 m/s. What is the centripetal force?
explanation_steps: F = mv²/r = 2 × 9 / 0.5 = 36 N, directed towards the centre.

questions.stem: Assume that objects 'a' and 'b' are placed in thermal contact and separately in thermal equilibrium with a third object 'c' that is at 70°C. The temperature of 'a' in °C is
explanation_steps: Zeroth law of thermodynamics: if two bodies are each in thermal equilibrium with a third body, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other – all three have the same temperature (G10 pp.41–43).
So a is at 70 °C. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: The zeroth law of thermodynamics is the basis of
explanation_steps: A thermometer reads the temperature of a body because it comes into thermal equilibrium with it. Answer: B.

questions.stem: A heat engine undergoes a process in which it absorbs 1500 J of heat and at the same time does 600 J of work. The change in internal energy of the heat engine, in joules, is
explanation_steps: First law of thermodynamics: ΔU = Q − W, with Q = heat absorbed and W = work done by the system (G10 pp.87–88).
ΔU = 1500 − 600 = 900 J. Answer: E. (2100 J wrongly adds the work.)

similar_questions.stem: A gas absorbs 400 J of heat while 150 J of work is done ON it. What is the change in its internal energy?
explanation_steps: Work done on the gas: W = −150 J, so ΔU = Q − W = 400 − (−150) = 550 J.

options.D: A 250 W TV set in 1 h

explanation_steps: Energy = power × time (G10 pp.196–199); the 220 V is not needed.
The TV uses the most energy (0.25 kWh). Answer: D.

questions.stem: The image produced by a pinhole camera is

options.B: sharply focused if the hole is big.
options.C: blurred if the hole is small.

explanation_steps: Light travels in straight lines through the pinhole, so rays from the top of the object reach the bottom of the screen: the image is real (formed on a screen) and inverted (G10 pp.212–215).
A bigger hole makes the image brighter but blurred; a small hole gives a sharper image. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: A pinhole camera is 10 cm long. A tree 20 m high is 50 m away. How high is the image?
explanation_steps: Image height / object height = image distance / object distance → h = 20 m × 0.10 / 50 = 0.04 m = 4 cm.

questions.stem: An object that is placed 40 cm in front of a plane mirror moves at a constant speed of 4 cm/s away from the mirror. The distance, in centimeters, between the image and the object after 10 seconds is
explanation_steps: After 10 s the object has moved 4 × 10 = 40 cm further away, so it is 40 + 40 = 80 cm from the mirror (G10 pp.223–228).
A plane mirror forms the image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front: 80 cm. Object–image distance = 80 + 80 = 160 cm. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: A girl stands 3 m in front of a plane mirror and walks towards it at 0.5 m/s. How far is she from her image after 2 s?
explanation_steps: She moves 1 m and is now 2 m from the mirror; the image is 2 m behind it; separation = 4 m.

explanation_steps: Light from the bottom bends away from the normal as it passes from water into air (refraction), so the bottom appears raised: apparent depth = real depth / n (G11 pp.11–14).

questions.stem: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a diverging lens that produces a magnification of 0.8. The power of the lens, in dioptres, is
explanation_steps: A diverging lens gives a virtual, upright, diminished image on the same side as the object. m = di/do → |di| = 0.8 × 30 = 24 cm; the image is virtual, so di = −24 cm (G11 pp.26–30).
P = 1/f (in metres) = 1/(−1.20) = −0.83 D. Answer: E. (−1.20 is the focal length in metres, not the power.)
tips: Power in dioptres needs f in metres; a diverging lens has negative f and negative power.

similar_questions.stem: A converging lens has a focal length of 25 cm. What is its power?
explanation_steps: P = 1/f = 1/0.25 m = +4 dioptres.

questions.stem: Which of the following does not produce a magnetic field?
explanation_steps: Magnetic fields are produced by moving charges: electric currents, moving charged particles, the orbital motion and spin of electrons in atoms (the origin of permanent magnetism) (G11 pp.80–82, 90).
A charge at rest produces only an electric field. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Who first showed that an electric current produces a magnetic field (a compass needle is deflected near a wire)?
explanation_steps: Hans Christian Oersted (1820). Answer: B.

questions.stem: Two conducting coils are brought close together. An emf is induced in one of the coils due to the change in the

options.A: number of turns of the other coil.
options.D: number of turns of the coil.

explanation_steps: Mutual induction: a changing current in one coil produces a changing magnetic flux that links the second coil, inducing an emf in it (Faraday's law) (G11 pp.125–128).
Answer: C. (A steady current, however large, induces nothing.)

similar_questions.stem: Why does a transformer not work with steady direct current?

options.B: A steady current produces no change of magnetic flux
options.C: DC flows only in one coil

explanation_steps: Induction needs a changing flux; steady DC gives a constant flux, so no emf is induced in the secondary. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The amplitude of the new wave produced by constructive interference of two waves is

options.A: equal to the amplitude of either of the waves.
options.B: greater than the amplitude of either of the waves.
options.C: less than the least amplitude of either of the waves.
options.D: equal to the sum of the amplitudes of the waves.
options.E: equal to the difference between the amplitudes of the waves.

explanation_steps: Principle of superposition: when crest meets crest (in phase), the displacements add, so the resultant amplitude = A₁ + A₂ (G11 pp.174–176).
D is keyed as the exact statement. B is also true (the sum is greater than either amplitude), so B is also accepted. E describes destructive interference.

similar_questions.stem: Two waves of amplitudes 3 cm and 5 cm meet exactly out of phase. What is the resultant amplitude?
explanation_steps: Destructive interference: A = |5 − 3| = 2 cm.

questions.review_flag: D (sum of amplitudes) is keyed, but B (greater than either amplitude) is also a true statement of constructive interference, so B is accepted as well.

questions.stem: A point source of sound emits sound energy at a rate of 60 W. If this emitted energy passes through a spherical surface of radius 20 cm, then the intensity of the sound at the surface, in W/m², is
explanation_steps: Intensity = power / area; a point source spreads its power over a sphere of area 4πr² (G11 pp.201–203).

similar_questions.stem: A 100 W point source emits sound uniformly. What is the intensity 2 m away?

questions.stem: Currents are induced in a television antenna by
explanation_steps: Television and radio broadcasts use radio waves (VHF/UHF bands). Their oscillating electric field drives electrons in the metal antenna, inducing an alternating current (G11 pp.213–218).
Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Which electromagnetic waves have the longest wavelength?
explanation_steps: Radio waves are at the long-wavelength (low-frequency) end of the EM spectrum. Answer: E.

questions.stem: The force of a wind is greater if the

options.A: wind blows from east to west.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p.39): 'The differences in pressure of any weather give rise to winds. The greater the pressure difference, the greater is the force of the wind.'
Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Lines on a weather map joining places of equal atmospheric pressure are called
explanation_steps: Isobars join points of equal pressure; closely spaced isobars mean strong winds. Answer: B.

questions.stem: In a hydraulic lever, a force of 25 N acts on the small piston of radius 7 cm. The force exerted by the liquid on the larger piston of radius 28 cm, in N, is
explanation_steps: Pascal's principle: the pressure is transmitted equally, so F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂ and F₂ = F₁ × (r₂/r₁)² (G12 pp.54–57).
F₂ = 25 × (28/7)² = 25 × 16 = 400 N. Answer: E. (100 N wrongly uses the ratio of radii instead of areas.)
tips: Area ∝ r², so doubling the radius multiplies the force by 4.

explanation_steps: Balanced columns in a U-tube exert equal pressures at the same level: h₁ρ₁g = h₂ρ₂g (G12 pp.16–17).

questions.stem: The number of electrons in an ionized atom is

options.A: equal to the number of protons in the atom.
options.B: equal to the number of neutrons in the atom.
options.C: less than the number of protons in the atom.
options.D: different from the number of protons in the atom.
options.E: greater than the number of protons in the atom.

explanation_steps: A neutral atom has equal numbers of electrons and protons. An ion (ionised atom) has either lost electrons (positive ion: fewer electrons than protons) or gained electrons (negative ion: more electrons) (G12 pp.93–94).
The statement true for every ion is D (different from the number of protons). Answer: D.
C is also accepted: in physics 'ionisation' usually means removing an electron (e.g. by radiation or ionisation energy), which leaves fewer electrons than protons.

similar_questions.stem: An atom with 11 protons and 10 electrons is
explanation_steps: It has one more proton than electrons, so it carries a charge of +1 (Na⁺). Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: D (different from the number of protons) is true for all ions and is keyed; C is also accepted because 'ionised' commonly means an electron has been removed.
